questions.question: In a eukaryotic cell observed under a microscope, the three main components visible are:

options.text: endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body and nucleoid

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**plasma membrane, nucleus and cytoplasm**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Every **eukaryotic cell**, whether plant or animal, displays three basic structural features when observed under a standard microscope: the **plasma membrane**, the **nucleus**, and the **cytoplasm**.
 
• The **plasma membrane** is the outermost boundary of the cell that separates the internal contents from the external environment. It is **selectively permeable**, meaning it regulates the entry and exit of specific substances. ***Hence, this component is part of the correct answer.***
 
• The **nucleus** is a prominent, usually spherical organelle that contains the **genetic material (DNA)** of the organism. It acts as the **control center** for cellular activities like growth and reproduction. ***Hence, this component is part of the correct answer.***
 
• The **cytoplasm** is the **translucent, jelly-like substance** found between the plasma membrane and the nuclear envelope. It houses various specialized **organelles** and is the site for most **metabolic reactions**. ***Hence, this component is part of the correct answer.***
 
• Other structures like the **nucleoid** and **capsule** are characteristic features of **prokaryotic cells** (such as **bacteria**) and are not found in eukaryotic cells. ***Hence, options 2 and 3 are incorrect.***
 
• While **ribosomes** and **vacuoles** are present in eukaryotic cells, they are often considered secondary organelles or are too small to be identified as one of the "three main components" compared to the fundamental structure of the membrane, nucleus, and cytoplasm. ***Hence, option 1 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Plasma Membrane:**
 
 
• It is primarily composed of a **phospholipid bilayer** interspersed with **proteins** and **cholesterol**.
 
• Its thickness ranges from **5 to 10 nanometers** and it follows the **Fluid Mosaic Model** proposed by **Singer and Nicolson** in **1972**.
 
 
 
• **Nucleus:**
 
 
• It was first discovered and described by the scientist **Robert Brown** in the year **1831**.
 
• It contains **chromosomes**, which are made of **DNA** and **histone proteins**. The nucleus is bounded by a **double membrane** called the **nuclear envelope**.
 
 
 
• **Cytoplasm:**
 
 
• The liquid part of the cytoplasm is called **cytosol**, which consists of **80% water**, salts, and organic molecules.
 
• It provides the **turgidity** to the cell and facilitates the **movement of materials** through cytoplasmic streaming.
 
 
 
• **Eukaryotic vs. Prokaryotic Cells:**
 
 
• **Eukaryotes** have a **well-defined nucleus** and **membrane-bound organelles** (e.g., humans, plants, fungi).
 
• **Prokaryotes** lack a nuclear membrane; their genetic material is naked in a region called the **nucleoid** (e.g., **E. coli** bacteria).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cell Wall:** While present in **plant cells**, it is **absent in animal cells**. Therefore, it cannot be considered a universal "main component" for all eukaryotic cells.
 
• **Cell Theory:** Proposed by **M.J. Schleiden** (**1838**) and **Theodore Schwann** (**1839**), it states that all living organisms are composed of cells and the cell is the **basic unit of life**.
 
• **Microscopy:** Most organelles like **mitochondria** or **ribosomes** require an **electron microscope** for detailed viewing, whereas the **nucleus** and **cell boundary** are often visible under a **compound light microscope**.
</ul

questions.question: A ray of light parallel to the principal axis, after reflection from a concave mirror, _________.

options.text: passes through the centre of curvature

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**passes through the principal focus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When a ray of light is **parallel** to the **principal axis** of a **concave mirror**, it always **passes through the principal focus (F)** after **reflection**. ***Hence, option 3 is correct.***
 
• A **concave mirror** is a **spherical mirror** whose **reflecting surface** is curved **inwards**, meaning it faces towards the **center of the sphere**.
 
• Because of its ability to **converge** parallel rays of light at a single point, the **concave mirror** is also widely known as a **converging mirror**.
 
• The point on the **principal axis** where all parallel incident rays meet after **reflection** is defined as the **principal focus** of the mirror.
 
• This behavior is consistent with the **laws of reflection**, where the **angle of incidence** is equal to the **angle of reflection** at the point of impact on the **curved surface**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Terminology of Spherical Mirrors:**
 
 
• **Pole (P):** The **geometric center** of the **reflecting surface** of a spherical mirror.
 
• **Centre of Curvature (C):** The **center of the sphere** of which the mirror's reflecting surface forms a part.
 
• **Principal Axis:** An **imaginary straight line** passing through the **pole** and the **centre of curvature** of the mirror.
 
• **Radius of Curvature (R):** The **distance** between the **pole** and the **centre of curvature**.
 
• **Focal Length (f):** The **distance** between the **pole** and the **principal focus**. For mirrors with small apertures, the relationship is **R = 2f**.
 
 
 
• **Convex Mirror Behavior:** In a **convex mirror** (diverging mirror), a ray **parallel** to the **principal axis** appears to **diverge** from the **principal focus** located **behind** the mirror.
 
• **Applications of Concave Mirrors:** They are commonly used in **shaving mirrors** to see an enlarged image, in **torches** and **car headlights** to get powerful parallel beams of light, and in **solar furnaces** to concentrate sunlight.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Standard Ray Rules for Image Formation:**
 
 
• **Rule 1:** A ray **parallel** to the **principal axis** passes through the **focus** after reflection.
 
• **Rule 2:** A ray passing through the **principal focus** will emerge **parallel** to the **principal axis** after reflection.
 
• **Rule 3:** A ray passing through the **centre of curvature** is reflected back along the **same path** because it strikes the mirror **normally** (at **90 degrees**).
 
• **Rule 4:** A ray incident obliquely to the **principal axis**, towards the **pole**, is reflected **obliquely** following the **laws of reflection**.
 
 
 
• **Image Characteristics:** Depending on the **position of the object**, a **concave mirror** can produce **real and inverted** images or **virtual and erect** images (when the object is between **P and F**).
</ul

questions.question: The sensation of feeling full after eaten enough is perceived in which part of our body?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fore-brain**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Fore-brain** (Prosencephalon) is the largest and most complex part of the human brain, serving as the main thinking part and the center for perceiving various sensations, including the feeling of being full (**satiety**).
 
• Within the **Fore-brain**, the **Hypothalamus** plays a critical role in maintaining **homeostasis**. It contains specialized centers that control **hunger** and **thirst**.
 
• A specific region known as the **satiety center** is located in the **ventromedial nuclei** of the **hypothalamus**. When we have eaten enough, this center is activated to suppress the desire for more food. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• The **Fore-brain** processes sensory information from various parts of the body. When the stomach is distended after a meal, neural signals are transmitted to the **brain**, which the **Fore-brain** interprets as the sensation of fullness.
 
• Apart from hunger, the **Fore-brain** is responsible for **voluntary actions**, **intelligence**, **memory**, **emotions**, and the regulation of **body temperature**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mid-brain (Mesencephalon):**
 
 
• The **Mid-brain** connects the **fore-brain** and the **hind-brain**. It is primarily involved in controlling **reflex movements** of the head, neck, and trunk in response to **visual** and **auditory** stimuli.
 
• It does not possess the higher-order centers required for interpreting metabolic states like **satiety**.
 
 
 
• **Buccal Cavity:**
 
 
• The **Buccal cavity**, or oral cavity, is the beginning of the **alimentary canal**. Its primary functions are **ingestion**, **mastication** (chewing) of food, and the initiation of **carbohydrate digestion** through **salivary amylase**.
 
• While it provides sensory feedback regarding taste and texture, the "perception" of being full is a **neurological process** occurring in the **central nervous system**, not the mouth.
 
 
 
• **Heart:**
 
 
• The **Heart** is a muscular organ responsible for pumping **oxygenated blood** to the tissues and **deoxygenated blood** to the lungs.
 
• It belongs to the **circulatory system** and does not have a role in the cognitive perception of hunger or satiety.
 
 
 
• **Hind-brain (Rhombencephalon):**
 
 
• Consists of the **Pons**, **Cerebellum**, and **Medulla Oblongata**. The **Medulla** controls involuntary actions like **heartbeat**, **breathing**, and **blood pressure**, while the **Cerebellum** maintains **body balance** and **posture**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hormonal Regulation:** The sensation of fullness is heavily influenced by hormones. **Leptin**, produced by **adipose (fat) tissue**, signals the **hypothalamus** in the **Fore-brain** to decrease appetite. Conversely, **Ghrelin**, produced by the stomach, signals hunger.
 
• **Neural Pathway:** The **Vagus nerve** (the **10th cranial nerve**) acts as a vital communication link between the **digestive tract** and the **brain**, carrying information about stomach stretch and nutrient levels to the **satiety centers**.
 
• **Cerebrum:** This part of the **Fore-brain** allows us to consciously realize we are full and make the **voluntary decision** to stop eating.
</ul

questions.question:
Consider the following statements and select the correct option.

Statement A: Baking soda is a mild non-corrosive basic salt.
Statement B: It can neutralise acids and relieve stomach acidity.

options.text: Both statements A and B are correct.
Both statements A and B are incorrect.
Statement A is correct but B is incorrect.
Statement A is incorrect but B is correct.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both statements A and B are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Baking soda** is chemically known as **Sodium Hydrogen Carbonate** or **Sodium Bicarbonate**, represented by the formula **NaHCO₃**.
 
• It is produced on a large scale using the **Solvay process**, where **Sodium Chloride** reacts with **Ammonia**, **Water**, and **Carbon Dioxide**.
 
• It is a **mild non-corrosive basic salt**. It is considered a salt of a strong base (**Sodium Hydroxide**) and a weak acid (**Carbonic Acid**), which gives it its basic properties. ***Hence, statement A is correct.***
 
• Because of its basic nature, it acts as an **antacid**. When consumed in small quantities, it reacts with the **Hydrochloric acid** present in the stomach to produce salt, water, and **Carbon Dioxide**, thereby neutralizing the excess acid. ***Hence, statement B is correct.***
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Both statements A and B are correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Uses in the Food Industry:**
 
 
• **Baking soda** is a key component of **baking powder**, which is a mixture of baking soda and a mild edible acid like **tartaric acid**.
 
• When **baking powder** is heated or mixed with water, it releases **Carbon Dioxide** gas, which makes bread and cakes **soft and spongy** by creating small air bubbles.
 
 
 
• **Chemical Reactions:**
 
 
• When **Sodium Hydrogen Carbonate** is heated during cooking, it undergoes thermal decomposition to form **Sodium Carbonate** (**Na₂CO₃**), **Water** (**H₂O**), and **Carbon Dioxide** (**CO₂**).
 
• The chemical equation is: **2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂**.
 
 
 
• **Fire Safety:**
 
 
• It is extensively used in **soda-acid fire extinguishers**. The reaction between the carbonate and acid releases a large volume of **CO₂**, which helps in extinguishing the fire by cutting off the oxygen supply.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Physical Properties:** **Baking soda** appears as a **white crystalline solid**, but it often looks like a fine powder. It has a slightly **alkaline (bitter) taste**.
 
• **pH Level:** The **pH** of a **Sodium Bicarbonate** solution is approximately **8.3**, confirming its status as a **weak base**.
 
• **Medicinal Use:** It is used to treat **acid indigestion** and **heartburn** because of its rapid **neutralization** effect on gastric acids.
 
• **Other Applications:** It is also used as a **water softener** in laundry, a **mild abrasive** for cleaning teeth, and for removing **odors** from refrigerators.
</ul

questions.question: What quantity is measured in cubic centimetres (cm³) ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Volume**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The quantity measured in **cubic centimetres (cm3)** is **Volume**. It represents the amount of **three-dimensional space** occupied by an object or a substance.
 
• A **cubic centimetre** is a unit of volume that corresponds to the volume of a **cube** that measures **1 cm x 1 cm x 1 cm**.
 
• In the **CGS (Centimetre-Gram-Second)** system of units, the cubic centimetre was the base unit for volume. While the **SI (International System of Units)** uses **cubic metres (m3)** as the standard unit, the **cm3** remains widely used in chemistry, medicine, and automotive engine displacement.
 
• There is a direct relationship between metric units of volume and capacity: **1 cm3** is exactly equal to **1 millilitre (mL)**.
 
• In medicine, the term **"cc"** is often used as an abbreviation for cubic centimetre, particularly when measuring **dosages** of liquid medications.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mass**:
 
 
• **Mass** is a measure of the amount of **matter** contained in an object.
 
• The **SI unit** for mass is the **kilogram (kg)**, though **grams (g)** and **milligrams (mg)** are frequently used for smaller quantities.
 
• Unlike weight, mass is an **intrinsic property** and does not change regardless of the **gravitational field** the object is placed in.
 
 
 
• **Temperature**:
 
 
• **Temperature** is a physical quantity that expresses the degree of **hotness or coldness** of a substance.
 
• The **SI unit** is **Kelvin (K)**. Other commonly used scales include **Celsius (C)** and **Fahrenheit (F)**.
 
• It is a measure of the **average kinetic energy** of the particles in a system.
 
 
 
• **Pressure**:
 
 
• **Pressure** is defined as the **force** applied perpendicular to the surface of an object per unit **area** over which that force is distributed.
 
• The **SI unit** for pressure is the **Pascal (Pa)**, which is equivalent to **1 Newton per square metre (N/m2)**.
 
• Other units include **atmosphere (atm)**, **bar**, and **millimetres of mercury (mmHg)**.
 
 
 
• **Volume Conversions**:
 
 
• **1,000 cubic centimetres** are equal to **1 Litre (L)**.
 
• **1 cubic metre (m3)** is equal to **1,000,000 cubic centimetres**.
 
• The **density** of a substance is calculated by dividing its **mass** by its **volume** (Density = Mass/Volume), with common units being **g/cm3**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Measurement Tools**: The volume of liquids is typically measured using **graduated cylinders**, **beakers**, **pipettes**, or **burettes**.
 
• **Archimedes' Principle**: For **irregularly shaped solids**, volume can be determined using the **water displacement method**. The volume of the displaced water is equal to the volume of the submerged object.
 
• **State of Matter**: While solids and liquids have a **fixed volume** at a given temperature and pressure, the volume of a **gas** will expand to fill whatever **container** it is placed in.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following correctly represents the total number of atoms in one molecule of ammonium sulphate ((NH₄)₂SO₄) ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**15**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The chemical formula for **Ammonium Sulphate** is **(NH4)2SO4**. To find the total number of atoms, we must sum the atoms of each individual element present in **one molecule** of the compound.
 
• The formula contains the **ammonium ion** **(NH4)** enclosed in parentheses with a **subscript 2**. This indicates that there are **two units** of the ammonium group.
 
• Inside one **NH4** group, there is **1 Nitrogen (N)** atom and **4 Hydrogen (H)** atoms, making a total of **5 atoms** per ammonium ion. Since there are two such groups, the total for the ammonium part is **2 × 5 = 10 atoms** (specifically, **2 Nitrogen** and **8 Hydrogen** atoms).
 
• The **sulphate ion** part of the formula is **SO4**. It consists of **1 Sulphur (S)** atom and **4 Oxygen (O)** atoms.
 
• Calculating the total atoms in the **sulphate** group: **1 (S) + 4 (O) = 5 atoms**.
 
• Adding the atoms from both parts together: **10 atoms** (from ammonium) + **5 atoms** (from sulphate) = **15 atoms**. ***Hence, the correct answer is 15.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chemical Nature and Properties**: **Ammonium Sulphate** is an **inorganic salt** that appears as a **white crystalline solid**. It is highly **soluble in water** but insoluble in alcohol.
 
• **Molar Mass**: The **molar mass** of **(NH4)2SO4** is approximately **132.14 g/mol**. This is calculated by adding the **atomic masses**: (2 × 14.01 for N) + (8 × 1.008 for H) + (1 × 32.06 for S) + (4 × 16.00 for O).
 
• **Commercial Uses**: Its primary use is as a **soil fertilizer**. It is particularly effective for **alkaline soils** as the ammonium ion is released and forms a small amount of acid, lowering the **pH balance** of the soil while contributing essential **Nitrogen** for plant growth.
 
• **Industrial Production**: It is produced by treating **ammonia** with **sulphuric acid (H2SO4)**. The reaction is represented as: **2NH3 + H2SO4 → (NH4)2SO4**.
 
• **Atomicity**: The total number of atoms present in a molecule of a substance is known as its **atomicity**. In this context, the **atomicity** of **Ammonium Sulphate** is **15**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Understanding Subscripts**: In chemical formulas, a **subscript** after a parenthesis multiplies every atom inside the parenthesis. For example, in **(NH4)2**, the **2** multiplies both the **1 Nitrogen** and the **4 Hydrogen** atoms.
 
• **Polyatomic Ions**: **Ammonium (NH4+)** and **Sulphate (SO4²-)** are examples of **polyatomic ions**, which are groups of atoms that stay together as a single charged unit during chemical reactions.
 
• **Valency and Balancing**: The formula **(NH4)2SO4** is derived because the **Ammonium ion** has a **valency of +1** and the **Sulphate ion** has a **valency of -2**. To create a **neutral compound**, two ammonium ions are needed for every one sulphate ion.
</ul

questions.question: Which roasting operation shown below burns out sulphur from a sulphide ore?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Oxidising**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Oxidising Roasting** is a metallurgical process where **sulphide ores** are heated to a high temperature (below their melting point) in the presence of an excess of **oxygen** or air.
 
• The primary objective of this operation is to burn out **sulphur** from the ore, which escapes as **sulphur dioxide (SO2)** gas. ***Hence, the option "Oxidising" is correct.***
 
• During this process, the metal sulphides are converted into **metal oxides** or **metal sulphates**, which are easier to reduce in subsequent stages of extraction.
 
• A classic example is the roasting of **Zinc Blende (ZnS)**, represented by the chemical equation: **2ZnS + 3O2 → 2ZnO + 2SO2**. In this reaction, the **sulphur** is effectively removed as a gaseous byproduct.
 
• This operation is typically carried out in a **Reverberatory Furnace** or a **Fluidized Bed Roaster**, where the temperature and air supply can be strictly controlled to ensure maximum oxidation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chloridising Roasting:**
 
 
• This involves heating the **ore** with a chlorinating agent, such as **Sodium Chloride (NaCl)** or **Chlorine gas**.
 
• It is used to convert certain metal compounds into **volatile or soluble chlorides**. This process is historically significant in the extraction of **Silver** (the **Patera process**) and **Copper**.
 
 
 
• **Volatilising Roasting:**
 
 
• In this operation, the ore is heated specifically to remove **volatile impurities** such as **Arsenic**, **Antimony**, and **Bismuth**.
 
• These impurities are converted into their respective **volatile oxides** (e.g., **As2O3**) which escape as vapours, leaving behind a purified ore residue.
 
 
 
• **Smelting:**
 
 
• **Smelting** is not a type of roasting but a subsequent stage in **pyrometallurgy**.
 
• It involves heating the roasted ore with a **reducing agent** (like **Coke**) and a **flux** at temperatures exceeding the **melting point** of the metal.
 
• The goal is to produce the molten metal and a byproduct called **slag**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Roasting vs. Calcination:** While **roasting** is used for **sulphide ores** in the presence of air, **calcination** is used for **carbonate** or **hydrated oxide ores**. **Calcination** involves heating the ore in the **absence** or limited supply of air to remove **carbon dioxide** or moisture.
 
• **Environmental Impact:** The **sulphur dioxide (SO2)** released during **oxidising roasting** is a major air pollutant. In modern plants, this gas is captured and used to manufacture **Sulphuric Acid (H2SO4)** to prevent acid rain and environmental degradation.
 
• **Temperature Control:** It is **crucial** that the temperature during roasting does not reach the **melting point** of the ore, as fusion would prevent the air from reacting with the inner parts of the ore particles.
</ul

questions.question: The pattern formed by iron filings around a bar magnet demonstrates ___________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**magnetic field lines**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The pattern formed by **iron filings** around a **bar magnet** is a visual representation of the **magnetic field lines**. These filings align themselves along the lines of force existing in the space surrounding the magnet.
 
• When **iron filings** are sprinkled on a surface near a magnet, each tiny piece of iron acts like a **small magnetic compass**. Due to **magnetic induction**, they become magnetized and align their long axes parallel to the direction of the **magnetic field** at that point.
 
• The **magnetic field** is a region around a magnetic material or a moving electric charge within which the force of magnetism acts. Since the field is invisible, the filings serve as a practical tool to observe its **shape** and **direction**.
 
• The **density** or closeness of the lines in the pattern indicates the **strength** of the magnetic field. The filings are most concentrated at the **poles** (North and South), showing that the magnetic force is strongest at these points.
 
• Magnetic field lines are **continuous loops**. Outside the magnet, the direction of these lines is taken to be from the **North pole** to the **South pole**, while inside the magnet, they travel from the **South pole** to the **North pole**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Magnetic Field (B):** It is a **vector quantity**, meaning it has both **magnitude** and **direction**. The **SI unit** of magnetic field strength is the **Tesla (T)**, named after **Nikola Tesla**.
 
• **Electric Field Lines:** These represent the path a positive test charge would follow in an electric field. Unlike magnetic lines, **electric field lines** originate from **positive charges** and end at **negative charges**; they do not typically form closed loops.
 
• **Electrostatic Force:** This is the **attractive** or **repulsive** force between particles caused by their **electric charges**. It is governed by **Coulomb's Law**, which was formulated in **1785**.
 
• **Gravitational Field Lines:** These represent the **gravitational force** exerted by a mass. Gravitational lines always point **inward** toward the center of the mass, as gravity is strictly an **attractive force**.
 
• **Bar Magnet:** A common type of **permanent magnet** usually made of **Alnico** (an alloy of Aluminum, Nickel, and Cobalt) or **Ferrite**. It always has **two poles**, and if broken in half, each piece will still possess both a North and a South pole.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Properties of Magnetic Field Lines:**
 
 
• They **never intersect** or cross each other. If they did, it would imply that at the point of intersection, the magnetic field has two different directions, which is physically impossible.
 
• The **relative strength** of the magnetic field is shown by the degree of **closeness** of the field lines.
 
• The tangent drawn at any point on a field line gives the **direction** of the magnetic field at that specific point.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:** The concept of field lines was introduced by **Michael Faraday** in the **19th century**. He referred to them as "lines of force" to explain how magnets and charges interact over a distance without physical contact.
 
• **Comparison with Earth:** The **Earth** itself acts like a giant bar magnet with its own **magnetic field lines**. This is why a **magnetic compass** needle, which is a small magnet, aligns itself with the Earth's magnetic North and South poles.
</ul

questions.question: What happens to a substance when it is reduced in a reaction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It gains electrons**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Reduction** is a fundamental chemical process where a substance **gains one or more electrons** during a reaction. This process is the opposite of **oxidation**, which involves the loss of electrons.
 
• In terms of **oxidation states**, reduction results in a **decrease in the oxidation number** of the atom or ion. For example, if a **Copper(II) ion (Cu²⁺)** gains **two electrons**, it is reduced to **metallic Copper (Cu⁰)**, reducing its oxidation state from **+2 to 0**.
 
• A substance that undergoes reduction acts as the **oxidizing agent**. This is because it facilitates the oxidation of another substance by **accepting or "pulling" electrons** away from it.
 
• The concept of electron transfer is often remembered using the mnemonic **OIL RIG**, which stands for **Oxidation Is Loss** and **Reduction Is Gain** (of electrons).
 
• In biological and classical chemistry, reduction can also be described as the **gain of Hydrogen** or the **loss of Oxygen** from a molecule. ***Hence, the statement that it gains electrons is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Redox Reactions**: Reduction and oxidation always occur **simultaneously** in a chemical reaction; such reactions are termed **Redox reactions**. Electrons lost by one species are immediately gained by another.
 
• **Reducing Agent**: The substance that **donates electrons** is called the **reducing agent** (or reductant). It gets oxidized in the process. For instance, in the reaction between **Zinc and Copper Sulfate**, Zinc acts as the reducing agent.
 
• **Oxidation (Option 4)**: This is the chemical process where an atom or molecule **loses electrons**. This leads to an **increase in the oxidation state**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• **Protons (Option 2)**: Chemical reactions involve the transfer or sharing of **valence electrons**, not **protons**. The number of protons determines the identity of the element and remains constant in the **nucleus** during a standard chemical reaction. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Reactivity (Option 1)**: While reduction changes the chemical nature of a substance, it does not universally mean it becomes "more reactive." Often, ions are reduced to their **stable elemental forms**, which may be less reactive. ***Hence, statement 1 is not the defining characteristic.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Definition**: Originally, **reduction** referred to the "reduction" of metal ores to pure metals, which typically involved the **removal of oxygen** (e.g., reducing **Iron Oxide** to **Iron** using carbon).
 
• **Mnemonic Devices**: Apart from **OIL RIG**, another popular mnemonic is **LEO the lion says GER**, which stands for **Loss of Electrons is Oxidation** and **Gain of Electrons is Reduction**.
 
• **Applications**: Reduction is vital in **electroplating**, **battery technology** (where reduction occurs at the **cathode**), and biological processes like **photosynthesis** and **cellular respiration**.
 
• **Electronegativity**: More **electronegative** elements, such as **Fluorine** and **Oxygen**, have a high tendency to undergo reduction because they strongly attract electrons.

questions.question: What happens to the uterus lining if the egg is not fertilised?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Failure of Menstruation:** If a woman misses her period, it is often the first **clinical sign** of **pregnancy**, although it can also be caused by **stress**, **hormonal imbalances**, or **nutritional deficiencies**.

questions.question: Which of the following reactions is an example of a reduction reaction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Reduction Reaction**: In classical chemistry, **reduction** is defined as the **removal of oxygen** from a substance or the **addition of hydrogen** to a substance.
 
• In the reaction **CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O**, **Copper(II) Oxide (CuO)** reacts with **Hydrogen gas (H2)**. During this process, **CuO** loses its **Oxygen** atom to become metallic **Copper (Cu)**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• Simultaneously, the **Hydrogen (H2)** gains the oxygen lost by the copper oxide to form **Water (H2O)**. This gain of oxygen is termed **oxidation**.
 
• Because both oxidation and reduction occur at the same time in this reaction, it is classified as a **Redox Reaction** (Reduction-Oxidation).
 
• In this specific example, **CuO** acts as the **oxidizing agent** (it provides oxygen), while **H2** acts as the **reducing agent** (it removes oxygen).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Oxidation Reaction**: 
 
 
• Oxidation is the **gain of oxygen** or the **loss of hydrogen**. In the reaction **2Mg + O2 → 2MgO**, **Magnesium** gains oxygen to form **Magnesium Oxide**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• This reaction is often demonstrated in laboratories by burning a magnesium ribbon in the air, producing a dazzling white flame.
 
 
 
• **Neutralization Reaction**:
 
 
• The reaction **NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O** is a **neutralization reaction** where a **Base (Sodium Hydroxide)** and an **Acid (Hydrochloric Acid)** react to form **Salt (Sodium Chloride)** and **Water**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• There is no change in the **oxidation state** of the elements involved in this specific acid-base reaction; therefore, it is not a redox process.
 
 
 
• **Displacement Reaction**:
 
 
• In **Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2**, **Zinc** displaces **Hydrogen** from **Sulphuric Acid**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• While this is a redox reaction (Zinc is oxidized from 0 to +2, and Hydrogen is reduced from +1 to 0), the primary focus of the question is to identify the classical example of **reduction** via the **loss of oxygen**, which is most clearly illustrated in the **CuO** example.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Electronic Concept of Reduction**: In modern chemistry, **reduction** is defined as the **gain of electrons** by an atom, ion, or molecule. A helpful mnemonic is **OIL RIG** (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).
 
• **Oxidation State**: In the reaction **CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O**, the **Copper** ion in **CuO** has an oxidation state of **+2**. After the reaction, the metallic **Copper (Cu)** has an oxidation state of **0**. This **decrease in oxidation number** is a clear indicator of **reduction**.
 
• **Applications**: **Reduction reactions** are fundamental in **metallurgy** for extracting pure metals from their ores. For instance, the reduction of **Iron Oxide** with **Carbon Monoxide** in a blast furnace is essential for **steel production**.
 
• **Reducing Agents**: Common reducing agents used in industrial and chemical processes include **Hydrogen (H2)**, **Carbon (C)**, **Carbon Monoxide (CO)**, and highly reactive metals like **Sodium (Na)** or **Aluminium (Al)**.

questions.question: During non-uniform motion of an object along a straight line _______.

options.text: the change in velocity over any time interval is zero.
the change in velocity over any time interval is non zero.
the velocity has same values at different points of the path.
the velocity remains constant with time.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**the change in velocity over any time interval is non zero**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Non-uniform motion** is defined as a type of motion where an object covers **unequal distances** in equal intervals of **time**, regardless of how small the time intervals are.
 
• In this type of motion, the **velocity** of the object does not remain constant; it changes as the object moves along a **straight line**. This means the **acceleration** of the object is **non-zero**.
 
• Because the **velocity** is constantly varying, the **change in velocity** (calculated as the difference between the final and initial velocity) over any specific **time interval** will result in a value other than zero. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• If the **change in velocity** were **zero**, it would imply that the initial and final velocities are identical, which characterizes **uniform motion** rather than non-uniform motion. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• In **non-uniform motion**, the object has **different velocities** at different points of its path because the speed or direction (or both) is changing. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• Since the definition of non-uniform motion involves a **variable rate** of displacement, the **velocity** cannot remain **constant** with time. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Velocity and its Nature**:
 
 
• **Velocity** is a **vector quantity**, meaning it has both **magnitude** (speed) and **direction**.
 
• The **SI unit** of velocity is **meters per second (m/s)**.
 
• In **rectilinear motion** (motion along a straight line), **non-uniformity** arises when the **speed** of the object changes over **time**.
 
 
 
• **Uniform vs. Non-Uniform Motion**:
 
 
• **Uniform Motion**: An object covers **equal distances** in equal intervals of **time**. The **velocity-time graph** for this motion is a **horizontal straight line** parallel to the time axis, and **acceleration** is **zero**.
 
• **Non-Uniform Motion**: The **distance-time graph** for this motion is a **curve** (parabolic or irregular), indicating that the **speed** is changing. Common **examples** include a **car** moving through a crowded **market** or a **train** starting from a **station**.
 
 
 
• **Acceleration**:
 
 
• **Acceleration** is the measure of the **rate of change of velocity**. It is calculated as **a = (v - u) / t**, where **v** is final velocity and **u** is initial velocity.
 
• In **non-uniform motion**, the **acceleration** is **non-zero**. It can be **uniform acceleration** (velocity changes by equal amounts in equal time) or **non-uniform acceleration** (velocity changes by unequal amounts in equal time).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Average and Instantaneous Velocity**:
 
 
• In **non-uniform motion**, the **instantaneous velocity** (velocity at a specific moment) is usually different from the **average velocity** (total displacement divided by total time).
 
• For a body in **non-uniform motion**, the **average speed** is often used to describe the overall rate of motion, as the **actual speed** fluctuates.
 
 
 
• **Real-world Examples**:
 
 
• A **stone** dropped from a building undergoes **uniformly accelerated non-uniform motion** due to **gravity** (acceleration of approximately **9.8 m/s²**).
 
• An **athlete** running a **100m race** exhibits **non-uniform motion** because they **accelerate** from rest and **decelerate** after crossing the finish line.
 
• A **bus** moving in **city traffic** is a classic example of **non-uniform motion** due to frequent stops and changes in **speed**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: When is the work done by a constant force on an object maximum?

options.text: When the force is opposite to the displacement
When the force is in the same direction as the displacement
When the force makes an angle of 45° with the displacement
When the force is perpendicular to the displacement

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**When the force is in the same direction as the displacement**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **work done** by a constant force on an object is mathematically defined as the product of the magnitude of the **force**, the magnitude of the **displacement**, and the **cosine of the angle** between the force and displacement vectors.
 
• The formula for work is expressed as **W = F s cos(theta)**, where **F** represents force, **s** represents displacement, and **theta** is the angle between them.
 
• When the force is in the **same direction** as the displacement, the angle **theta is 0 degrees**. Since the value of **cos(0) is 1**, the work done is **W = Fs**, which is the **maximum positive work** possible for a given force and displacement. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• When the force is **opposite** to the displacement (e.g., friction acting on a moving body), the angle **theta is 180 degrees**. Since **cos(180) is -1**, the work done is **negative (W = -Fs)**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• When the force makes an **angle of 45 degrees** with the displacement, the work done is calculated as **W = Fs cos(45)**. Since **cos(45) is approximately 0.707**, the work done is positive but significantly **less than the maximum** value. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• When the force is **perpendicular** to the displacement, the angle **theta is 90 degrees**. Since **cos(90) is 0**, the **work done is zero**, regardless of the magnitude of the force or displacement. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Nature of Work**: **Work** is a **scalar quantity**, which means it only has **magnitude** and no specific direction in space, even though it is derived from two **vector quantities** (force and displacement).
 
• **Units of Measurement**: In the **SI system** (International System of Units), the unit of work is the **Joule (J)**. One Joule is equal to **one Newton-meter (N-m)**. In the **CGS system**, work is measured in **ergs**, where **1 Joule equals 10⁷ ergs**.
 
• **Dimensions**: The **dimensional formula** for work is **[M1 L2 T-2]**. This is identical to the dimensions of **energy**, which aligns with the **Work-Energy Theorem** stating that work done on an object results in a change in its **kinetic energy**.
 
• **Types of Work**:
 
 
• **Positive Work**: Occurs when the force has a component in the direction of displacement (angle between **0 and 90 degrees**).
 
• **Negative Work**: Occurs when the force has a component opposite to the direction of displacement (angle between **90 and 180 degrees**).
 
• **Zero Work**: Occurs when there is **no displacement**, the **force is zero**, or the force and displacement are **mutually perpendicular**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Real-world Examples**:
 
 
• A person **lifting a box** vertically performs **positive work** because the upward force is in the same direction as the upward displacement.
 
• The **force of gravity** on a satellite moving in a circular orbit does **zero work** because the gravitational force is always **perpendicular** to the instantaneous displacement (velocity) of the satellite.
 
• A **coolie** walking on a horizontal platform with a load on his head does **no work against gravity** because the force he applies to hold the load is vertical, while the displacement is horizontal.
 
• **Brakes** applied to a moving car perform **negative work** because the braking force acts in the **opposite direction** to the car's motion.
 
 
 
• **Force-Displacement Graphs**: For a **variable force**, the work done can be calculated by finding the **area under the curve** in a Force-Displacement (F-s) graph.
</ul

questions.question: Cytoplasm is made up of an aqueous ground substance called:

__
 
• **Cytoplasm** is the jelly-like substance that fills the interior of a **cell** and is surrounded by the **plasma membrane**. It consists of the **cytosol**, **organelles**, and various **inclusions**.
 
• The **cytosol** is specifically the **aqueous ground substance** or the liquid component of the **cytoplasm** in which the organelles are suspended. ***Hence, the correct answer is cytosol.***
 
• It is a complex mixture of substances dissolved in **water**, which typically makes up about **70% to 90%** of its total volume.
 
• The **cytosol** contains dissolved **ions** (like **potassium**, **sodium**, and **magnesium**), small molecules (such as **glucose**, **amino acids**, and **nucleotides**), and large **water-soluble molecules** like **proteins** and **enzymes**.
 
• It serves as the site for several vital **metabolic pathways**, including **glycolysis**, **protein synthesis** (translation), and **cell division** (cytokinesis).
 
• The **cytosol** also plays a crucial role in providing **structural support** to the cell by housing the **cytoskeleton**, which maintains cell shape and enables **intracellular transport**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nucleoplasm:**
 
 
• This is the type of **protoplasm** found specifically within the **nucleus** of a **eukaryotic cell**.
 
• It is enclosed by the **nuclear envelope** and contains the **nucleolus** and **chromatin** (DNA and proteins).
 
• Its primary function is to serve as a suspension medium for the **genetic material** and to maintain the **nuclear shape**.
 
 
 
• **Chromoplasm:**
 
 
• **Chromoplasm** refers to the peripheral, pigmented portion of the **cytoplasm** found in certain **prokaryotic cells**, particularly **cyanobacteria** (blue-green algae).
 
• It contains **photosynthetic pigments** like **chlorophyll a**, **phycocyanin**, and **phycoerythrin** organized into **thylakoids**.
 
• It is distinct from the **centroplasm**, which is the colorless inner region containing the **DNA**.
 
 
 
• **Lysosomal Fluid:**
 
 
• This is the specialized fluid contained within **lysosomes**, which are membrane-bound **vesicles** used for **cellular digestion**.
 
• The fluid is highly **acidic**, typically maintaining a **pH of 4.5 to 5.0**, which is optimal for the activity of **hydrolytic enzymes** (acid hydrolases).
 
• These enzymes break down **macromolecules**, **damaged organelles**, and **foreign particles** like bacteria.
 
 
 
• **Protoplasm:**
 
 
• The term **protoplasm** is a general term used to describe the entire **living matter** of a cell, comprising both the **cytoplasm** and the **nucleus**.
 
• It was first coined by **J.E. Purkinje** in **1839** to denote the substance of the **animal embryo**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Read the given statements and select the most appropriate option.

Statement 1: When a ball is thrown vertically upward, its velocity decreases at the rate of g.
Statement 2: The acceleration due to gravity acts downward even when the ball moves upward.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both Statements 1 and 2 are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1**: When a ball is thrown **vertically upward**, it moves against the force of **gravity**. This force produces a constant **acceleration** directed toward the center of the Earth. Because the direction of **velocity** (upward) is opposite to the direction of **acceleration** (downward), the ball undergoes **retardation**. The **velocity** of the ball decreases at a constant rate of approximately **9.8 m/s²**, which is the value of **g**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 2**: **Gravity** is a **vector quantity** that always acts toward the **center of the Earth**, regardless of the object's state of motion. Whether the ball is moving **upward**, **downward**, or is momentarily at **rest** at its maximum height, the **acceleration due to gravity (g)** consistently acts **downward**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• At the **highest point** of the ball's trajectory, its **instantaneous velocity** becomes **zero**. However, the **acceleration** is not zero; it remains **9.8 m/s²** acting **downward**. If the acceleration were zero at the top, the ball would remain suspended in the air.
 
• The motion of the ball is a classic example of **uniformly accelerated motion** (or uniformly retarded motion during the ascent). The rate at which the **velocity** changes is defined by the **gravitational field strength** of the planet.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Both Statements 1 and 2 are correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Acceleration due to Gravity (g)**:
 
 
• On **Earth**, the average value of **g** is taken as **9.8 m/s²** or **32.2 ft/s²**.
 
• This value can vary slightly based on **latitude**, **altitude**, and local **geological structures**. It is slightly higher at the **poles** and lower at the **equator** due to the Earth's **rotation** and **oblate spheroid** shape.
 
 
 
• **Equations of Motion**:
 
 
• For an object thrown **upward**, the equations of motion are modified by replacing 'a' with **-g**.
 
• **v = u - gt** (Final velocity = Initial velocity - gravity * time).
 
• **h = ut - 1/2 gt²** (Height = Initial velocity * time - 0.5 * gravity * time squared).
 
• **v² = u² - 2gh**.
 
 
 
• **Symmetry of Vertical Motion**:
 
 
• In the absence of **air resistance**, the **time of ascent** (time to reach maximum height) is exactly equal to the **time of descent** (time to return to the starting level).
 
• The **speed** with which the ball is thrown **upward** will be equal to the **speed** with which it returns to the same **horizontal level**, though the **velocity** will have an opposite sign.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mass Independence**: The **acceleration due to gravity** is independent of the **mass** of the object. As famously demonstrated by **Galileo**, in a **vacuum**, a heavy ball and a light ball will fall (or be retarded when thrown up) at the **same rate**.
 
• **Vector Relationship**: **Velocity** and **acceleration** are both **vectors**. When they point in the **same direction**, the object **speeds up**; when they point in **opposite directions**, the object **slows down**. This is why the upward-moving ball slows down.
 
• **Sign Convention**: In **physics** problems, it is common to assign **upward** as the **positive (+)** direction and **downward** as the **negative (-)** direction. Under this convention, **velocity** is positive during ascent, and **acceleration (g)** is always **-9.8 m/s²**.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes fragmentation as a method of asexual reproduction?

options.text: The parent body breaks into pieces, and each piece grows into a new organism.
The parent organism divides into many cells which develop into spores.
A single cell divides into two identical daughter cells.
A new organism grows from a bud formed on the parent’s body.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The parent body breaks into pieces, and each piece grows into a new organism**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fragmentation** is a type of **asexual reproduction** where the body of a multicellular organism breaks into two or more distinct parts, each of which can grow into a complete new individual.
 
• This process is commonly observed in organisms with **simple body organization**, such as **Spirogyra** (a filamentous algae). Upon reaching maturity, the **Spirogyra** filament simply breaks into smaller pieces or fragments. ***Hence, the statement in option 1 is correct.***
 
• Unlike more complex organisms, these fragments undergo **mitosis** to develop into full-sized organisms that are genetically identical to the original parent, essentially acting as **clones**.
 
• **Fragmentation** differs from **regeneration** in that fragmentation is a standard method of reproduction used to increase population, whereas regeneration is often a mechanism to replace lost or damaged body parts.
 
• It is an efficient way for organisms like **fungi**, **lichens**, and certain **sea stars** to proliferate in favorable environmental conditions without the need for a mate.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Spore Formation (Option 2):**
 
 
• This method involves the parent organism producing microscopic, reproductive units called **spores**. These spores are often protected by a thick wall to survive unfavorable conditions.
 
• Examples include **Rhizopus** (bread mould) and **Mucor**. When conditions become favorable, the spores germinate into new individuals. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect regarding fragmentation.***
 
 
 
• **Binary Fission (Option 3):**
 
 
• This is the most common form of **asexual reproduction** in **unicellular organisms** like **Bacteria** and **Amoeba**.
 
• In this process, the **nucleus** and **cytoplasm** of a single cell divide into two equal halves, resulting in two identical daughter cells. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect regarding fragmentation.***
 
 
 
• **Budding (Option 4):**
 
 
• In **budding**, a small **outgrowth** or **bud** forms on the parent body due to repeated cell division at one specific site.
 
• These buds develop into tiny individuals and, when fully mature, detach from the parent body to become independent organisms. This is seen in **Hydra** and **Yeast**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect regarding fragmentation.***
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Asexual Reproduction** ensures rapid population growth as it does not involve the time-consuming process of finding a mate or the complex fusion of **gametes**.
 
• However, the lack of **genetic variation** makes the entire population vulnerable to environmental changes or diseases, as every individual is a genetic copy of the parent.
 
• In **Planaria** (flatworms), the organism exhibits a high degree of **regeneration**, where if it is cut into pieces, each piece can grow back into a complete worm. While similar to fragmentation, it is biologically categorized under specialized regenerative cells.
 
• Organisms like **Annelids** (earthworms) and **Echinoderms** (starfish) also utilize fragmentation as a means of accidental or intentional reproduction depending on the species and environmental triggers.
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about the direction of the magnetic field lines inside a current-carrying solenoid?

options.text: The magnetic field lines are circular and perpendicular to the axis of the solenoid.
The magnetic field lines are parallel and along the axis of the solenoid from its south pole to north pole.
The magnetic field lines are parallel and along the axis of the solenoid from its north pole to south pole.
The magnetic field lines are random inside the solenoid.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The magnetic field lines are parallel and along the axis of the solenoid from its south pole to north pole**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **solenoid** is a coil of many circular turns of **insulated copper wire** wrapped closely in the shape of a **cylinder**. When current passes through it, it behaves like a **bar magnet**.
 
• The magnetic field lines inside a current-carrying solenoid are **parallel straight lines**. This indicates that the **magnetic field** is **uniform** at all points inside the solenoid.
 
• The **direction** of the magnetic field lines inside the solenoid is from the **South pole to the North pole**. This completes the closed loops of the magnetic field lines. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• The magnetic field lines are not **circular** or **perpendicular** to the axis; they are directed **longitudinally** along the axis. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• While the lines outside the solenoid travel from **North to South**, the internal lines must travel from **South to North** to maintain continuity. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The magnetic field inside a solenoid is highly **organized** and **consistent**, not **random**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Uniform Magnetic Field:** The **parallel** nature of the field lines inside the solenoid signifies that the strength of the field does not vary from the **center** to the **internal edges**.
 
• **Electromagnets:** A strong magnetic field produced inside a solenoid can be used to **magnetize** a piece of magnetic material, such as a **soft iron core**, when placed inside the coil. The combination of the coil and the core is called an **electromagnet**.
 
• **Magnetic Field Strength:** The magnitude of the magnetic field (**B**) inside a long solenoid is given by the formula **B = μοnI**, where **μο** is the **permeability of free space**, **n** is the number of turns per unit length, and **I** is the **current**.
 
• **Polarity:** The ends of the solenoid act as **North** and **South** poles. One can determine the polarity using the **Clock Rule**; if the current appears to flow **clockwise** at one end, that end is the **South pole**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Factors Affecting Strength:** The strength of the magnetic field can be increased by increasing the **number of turns** in the coil, increasing the **magnitude of current**, or using a material with high **magnetic permeability** as a core.
 
• **Comparison with Bar Magnets:** Unlike a **permanent bar magnet**, the magnetic field of a solenoid can be switched **on or off** and its **polarity** can be reversed by changing the direction of the **current**.
 
• **Right-Hand Thumb Rule:** If you wrap your **right hand** around the solenoid with your fingers pointing in the direction of the **conventional current**, your thumb will point towards the **North pole** of the solenoid.
 
• **Applications:** Solenoids are widely used in **industrial applications**, including **relay switches**, **electric bells**, and **fuel injectors** in automobiles.
</ul

questions.question: Using cracked crockery to grow small plants is an example of ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Repurpose**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Repurposing** (also known as **creative reuse** or **upcycling**) is the process of taking an item that can no longer serve its **original function** and finding a **new use** for it. 
 
• In the given scenario, **cracked crockery** (such as cups, bowls, or pots) can no longer be used for its primary purpose of **dining or food storage** because the cracks may harbor bacteria or cause leaks. By using it to **grow small plants**, the item is given a **second life** in a completely different capacity. ***Hence, the correct answer is Repurpose.*** 
 
• **Reuse** refers to using an item **multiple times** for the **same purpose** for which it was originally intended, such as refilling a **glass water bottle**. Since the crockery is cracked and cannot be used for eating/drinking safely, it is not being "reused" in the strict sense. ***Hence, option 1 is incorrect.*** 
 
• **Recycle** involves **breaking down** a waste product into its **raw materials** to create a completely new product (e.g., melting down glass to make new jars). Using a cracked pot as a planter does not involve physical or chemical **reprocessing** of the material. ***Hence, option 2 is incorrect.*** 
 
• **Refuse** is the act of **declining** or saying no to items that are not needed, such as **single-use plastics** or promotional flyers, to prevent waste from being created in the first place. This does not apply to an item already in one's possession that has become damaged. ***Hence, option 4 is incorrect.*** 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **The Waste Hierarchy (5 Rs):** 
 
 
• The modern approach to **waste management** follows a hierarchy to minimize **environmental impact**. These are often listed as **Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, and Recycle**. 
 
• **Repurposing** sits higher than recycling in the hierarchy because it requires **less energy** and **no industrial processing**. 
 
 
 
• **Environmental Benefits of Repurposing:** 
 
 
• It reduces the volume of **solid waste** sent to **landfills**. 
 
• It conserves **natural resources** by delaying the need for new products. 
 
• It lowers **carbon emissions** because no manufacturing energy is consumed to create the "new" item (the planter). 
 
 
 
• **Common Examples of Repurposing:** 
 
 
• Turning **old tires** into garden swings or **furniture**. 
 
• Using **glass honey jars** to store **buttons or stationery**. 
 
• Converting **old t-shirts** into **cleaning rags**. 
 
• Using **plastic containers** as **organizers** for tools or hardware. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Circular Economy:** Repurposing is a fundamental pillar of a **circular economy**, where the goal is to keep **materials and products** in use for as long as possible. 
 
• **Sustainability:** By choosing to **repurpose** items like **cracked crockery**, individuals contribute to **sustainable living** practices. **Ceramics** are particularly good candidates for repurposing because they are **durable** but often difficult to **recycle** in standard municipal facilities. 
 
• **Distinction:** The key distinction between **Repurpose** and **Recycle** is that repurposing maintains the **physical integrity** of the object, while recycling destroys it to recover the **base material**. 
</ul
